parole.significato: body of churchmen that forms the chapter of a cathedral or collegiate church
parole.testo: From Late Latin capitulum, diminutive of Latin caput (“head”). Considering the /i/ < Latin /ĭ/, possibly an early borrowing or otherwise semi-learned (cf. French chapitre). Doublet of capítulo. Compare English chapter.

The confusion of y and ll in this term is already present in medieval texts, and Coromines and Pascual suspect i
Inherited from Latin grūmus (“heap”), from Proto-Indo-European *gar-, *ger- (“to tie, bind together”).
From Latin grunnītus.
Inherited from Latin grunnīre, probably ultimately imitative. Compare Portuguese grunhir, French grogner, Danish grynte, Old High German grunnizon, German grunzen.
From Latin gracilis.

Borrowed from Latin graphicus (“belonging to painting or drawing”), from Ancient Greek γραφικός (graphikós, “belonging to painting or drawing, picturesque, of or for writing; of style, lively”), from Proto-Indo-European *gerbʰ-.
Learned borrowing from Latin gravidus, from gravis (“heavy”).

Ultimately from Latin vappa (“flat wine, worthless person”), probably through the intermediate of dialectal Old French, namely Picard vape, wape, gape (“dull, insipid (of food); weakened (of people); deranged (of the stomach)”), which has possibly, but not necessarily received influence from Proto-G

parole.significato: to save (to store for future use)
parole.testo: Inherited from Early Medieval Latin wardāre.
Inherited from Early Medieval Latin warnīre.

Inherited from Old Spanish guay (“woe”), from Latin vae (“woe”) or Gothic 𐍅𐌰𐌹 (wai, “woe”), the latter from Proto-Germanic *wai, both from Proto-Indo-European *wai. Cognate with Portuguese guai, Catalan guai and Italian guai.

Inherited from Late Latin gulbia, gubia, from Gaulish *gulbiā, from Proto-Celtic *gulbā, *gulbīnos (“beak, bill”). See the late term for more information. Compare Middle Irish gulba (“beak”), English gouge.
Inherited from Latin vīticula, likely influenced by a Germanic word. Compare vedeja and vedija.
Inherited from Old Spanish guerra, from Early Medieval Latin werra, borrowed from Frankish *werʀu (“confusion; quarrel”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *werrizāre. Derivable from guerra (“war”) + -ear (verb-forming suffix).
Perhaps from Vulgar Latin *(petra) aquilea (“acute stone”), from aquileus (“acute”), from Latin aculeus.
From Lunfardo. Maybe from Latin wita (“to fine, mulct, punish”)
Deverbal from guiñar. Perhaps related to Late Latin cinnus (“scowl, wink”).
Borrowed from Latin gula. Compare the inherited doublet gola.

Inherited from Old Spanish gusano, of further uncertain origin. Possibly from Latin cossus (with an additional suffix), according to the Diccionario de la lengua española of 1884, but this is highly unlikely. Possibly from Paleo-Hispanic. Unrelated to Russian гу́сеница (gúsenica, “worm”). In the sen
Borrowed from Latin gustātiōnem.

parole.significato: translated as "to like", analyzable in structure as "to please" [with dative ‘someone’] (the thing being liked is the s…
parole.testo: Borrowed in this form from Latin gustāre. Replaced the inherited Old Spanish form gostar. See gusto. The use of this verb to mean "like" is a uniquely Ibero-Romance development. Compare Portuguese gostar.

Borrowed from Latin gustus (“taste”), from Proto-Italic *gustus, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵéwstus. Replaced the inherited Old Spanish form gosto. The learned word has a more abstract meaning overall.
From Latin galea.
Borrowed from Latin galgulus.
From Latin gallicus.
From Latin garrulus.
From Latin gelidus (“cold”), from gelū (“frost; chill”).
1st documentation: 1275. From Latin geminus.
Learned borrowing from Latin genus (through a regularized accusative *generum).
Borrowed from Latin genesis, from Ancient Greek γένεσις (génesis).

parole.significato: Gothic (of or relating to the Goths)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin gothicus (“gothic”).

parole.significato: broad bean, horse bean (Fabaceae, Vicia faba)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish faba, from Latin faba, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰabʰ- (“bean”). Cognate with English fava.
Unadapted borrowing from Latin habeas corpus ad subjiciendum (“You (shall) have the body to be subjected to (examination)”), see above for more details.
Unadapted borrowing from Ecclesiastical Latin habēmus (pāpam) (literally “we have (a pope)”).

parole.significato: to have; forms the perfect aspect
parole.testo: Latinised respelling of Old Spanish aver, from Latin habēre, habeō (“have, hold”), probably from Proto-Italic *habēō or *haβēō, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gʰeh₁bʰ- (“to grab, take”). Cognate with French avoir, Italian avere, Occitan aver, Portuguese haver, Romanian avea, avere, and Sardini
From Latin habilitātem. Cognate with English ability.

parole.significato: to enable (to give strength or ability to)
parole.testo: From Latin habilitāre.
Borrowed from Latin habitābilis.
From Latin habitātiōnem. By surface analysis, habitar + -ción.
From habitar + -dor, or possibly a borrowing from Latin habitātor.

parole.significato: to inhabit, to live or dwell in / on
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin habitāre. Cognate with English habit (“to clothe”) (v.).
From Latin habituālis.

parole.significato: to habituate; to be inured to, be accustomed to (by habit)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin habituāre. Compare English habituate.
From Latin habitūdō.
Inherited from Old Spanish fabla, from Latin fābula (“discourse”). Compare fábula, a borrowed doublet.
Inherited from Latin fābulāntem. By surface analysis, hablar (“to speak”) + -ante.

parole.significato: to talk; to speak; to communicate using words
parole.testo: From Old Spanish fablar, from Latin fābulārī (“chat, converse”). Doublet of fabular, which was borrowed from Latin.

Inherited from Old Spanish fazer, from Latin facere. The first-person indicative (hago) and present subjunctive forms (haga, hagas, etc.) may have been influenced by Latin agō (compare English gesture), but more likely come from a voicing of intervocalic Latin /k/ after having dropped /i/ (e.g. Lati

parole.significato: a kind of torch or large candle (often with four sticks)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish facha, from a Vulgar Latin *fascla, from syncopation of *fascula, presumably from a crossing of Latin facula and fascis. Doublet of fácula, a borrowing. Cognate with Old Galician-Portuguese facha.

According to Coromines and Pascual, from Old Spanish fazia (attested ca. 1300), with the variant faza (att. in Cid, Berceo, Calila e Dimna), and in pre-literary Latinized spelling faze ad (att. 1208, in a legal document), from Latin faciem ad (facing towards). Unlike in faz, the final -e of Latin fa
Inherited from Old Spanish fazienda, from Latin facienda (literally “things to be done”), from faciō (“to do”). Cognate with Portuguese fazenda. Doublet of faena.
From haz (“bundle”) + -ina, from Latin fascis.
From hacina (“stack, pile”) + -ar, from Latin fascis, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰask-. Compare Spanish fascia and faja.
From earlier fada, from Vulgar Latin *Fāta (“goddess of fate”), from the plural of Latin fātum (“fate”). Compare Catalan fada, Occitan fada, Portuguese fada, French fée, Italian fata.
Inherited from Latin fātum. Doublet of fado.
Borrowed from Latin haecceitās.

parole.significato: falcon (diurnal bird of prey in Falconidae and especially in Falco)
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Latin falcōnem, probably of Germanic origin. Doublet of falcón.
Inherited from Latin haliaeetus, from Ancient Greek ἁλιαίετος (haliaíetos).

parole.significato: to find something, deliberately or not
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish fallar (“to find”), following internal consonant spread and palatalization, namely via Vulgar Latin *faflāre, from Latin afflāre (“to breathe or blow upon”). Cognate to Portuguese achar, Romanian afla. For the phonetic development, compare Old Spanish finchar, Spanish hinc

By surface analysis, hallar + -azgo. Inherited from Old Spanish falladgo (13th c.), maybe from an unattested Vulgar Latin *afflāticum, from Latin afflō. Cognate with Galician and Portuguese achádego, Leonese chalga and Asturian ayalga.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin, from Latin halōs, from Ancient Greek ἅλως (hálōs, “disk of the sun or moon”).

Inherited from Old Spanish fambre, fanbre, famne (whence also Ladino ambre), from Vulgar Latin *faminem (the accusative of a nominative *famen or *famis), variant of Latin famēs, see there for more. For other examples of Latin /mVn/ > Old Spanish /mn/ > /mɾ/ > /mbɾ/ see hombre, nombre, muchedumbre,
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *faminentus, from Latin famēs. Cognate with Galician famento and Portuguese faminto.
Borrowed from Latin hāmus.
Inherited from Old Spanish farina, from Latin farīna (“flour”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰors-iHn-eh₂, from *bʰers-.
From harina + -ero or from Latin farīnārius. Cf. also harnero.

parole.significato: the hopper or drawer where grounded flour falls into
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *farināle, from Latin farīna.

parole.significato: to bore, tire, to make fed up
parole.testo: From Latin farcīre; and harto.
From Latin fartus (“stuffed”), from Latin farciō whence English farce. For sense evolution compare English fed up. Cognate with Galician farto, Portuguese farto, Asturian fartu and Catalan fart.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *fastigiāle, from Latin fastigium.
Inherited from Late Latin fastīdiāre, from Latin fastīdiō. Compare the borrowed doublet fastidiar. Compare English fash.
From hastío + -oso, or from Latin fastīdiōsus, and thus a doublet of the borrowed fastidioso.
Inherited from Latin fastīdium. Doublet of fastidio.
Inherited from Old Spanish faya, from Latin [materia] fāgea, from fāgus, from Proto-Italic *fāgos, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeh₂ǵos. Compare Galician and Portuguese faia.
From earlier haedo, inherited from Vulgar Latin *fāgētum, from Latin fāgus. Influenced by haya. Compare Asturian fayéu, Italian faggeto, Romanian făget.
Inherited from Latin fascis (“bundle”). Cognate with English fagot (“bundle of sticks, twigs or branches”). Doublet of fajo and feje.
Inherited from Old Spanish faz, from Latin faciēs. Doublet of facies and faz.
Inherited from Latin fascia (“band, strip, swathe”).
Borrowed from Latin hebdomada (“week”), from hebdomas (“seven, week”), from Ancient Greek ἑβδομάς (hebdomás, “the number seven”), from ἑπτά (heptá, “seven”).
Inherited from Old Spanish feviella~fiviella (with /e/ < /i/ perhaps via dissimilation), from Vulgar Latin *fībella, diminutive of Latin fībula. Compare Portuguese fivela, Galician fibela.
Inherited from Latin fibra. Compare the borrowed doublet fibra.
Borrowed from Latin hebraeus, from Ancient Greek Ἑβραῖος (Hebraîos), from Aramaic עִבְרַי (ʿiḇray), from Hebrew עִבְרִי (ʿiḇrī́).
Borrowed from Latin hecatombē.

Inherited from Old Spanish fechizo, from Latin factīcius (“artificial”, adjective), from factus (“made”) + -īcius. Compare the borrowed doublet facticio. Compare English factitious. Cognate with Portuguese feitiço.
Inherited from Latin factus. Doublet of facto.
From Latin factum n.
Inherited from Latin factor. Doublet of factor, which was borrowed.
Inherited from Latin factūra, from faciō + -tūra. Compare the borrowed doublet factura.
Inherited from Latin fētēre, probably from Proto-Indo-European *dʰewh₂-.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *fētibundus, from Latin fēteō, foeteō (“to have a bad smell, stink”). Compare the similar structured sabiondo.
Inherited from Old Spanish fedor, from Latin fētōrem.
From Early Medieval Latin gelāta, derived from Latin gelāre (“freeze”). By surface analysis, helar + -ada.

Inherited from Latin gelātus, perfect passive participle of Latin gelō (“to freeze”). Cognate to Italian gelato. By surface analysis, helar (“to freeze, to cool”) + -ado (past participle suffix). Literally, “frozen.”
Inherited from Latin gelāre.
Inherited from Old Spanish felecho, from Latin filictum (“fernbrake”), from filix (“fern”). Compare Asturian felechu, Friulian felet, Galician fieito, and Portuguese feto.
Borrowed from New Latin helium, from Ancient Greek ἥλιος (hḗlios, “sun”), because the element was first observed in the solar spectrum.
Borrowed from Latin Helvētius.
Borrowed from Latin helvēticus.
From Latin heliacus, from Ancient Greek ἡλιακός (hēliakós).

Inherited from Old Spanish femna, fembra, from Latin fēmina (“female”), from Proto-Italic *fēmanā, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁-m̥h₁n-eh₂ (“(f.) one who is sucked; one who suckles”), derivation of the verbal root *dʰeh₁(y)- (“to suck, suckle”). Doublet of fémina, which is a direct borrowing.

parole.significato: hemina (a Roman unit of liquid measure reckoned as the volume of ⁵⁄₆ Roman pound of wine, equivalent to around 0.27 L)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin hēmīna (“half-sextarius”), from Ancient Greek ἡμῑ́νᾱ (hēmī́nā).
From Latin hēmisphaerium, from Ancient Greek ἡμισφαίριον (hēmisphaírion), from ἡμι- (hēmi-, “half”) + σφαῖρα (sphaîra, “sphere”).
Borrowed from Late Latin hēmistichium, from Ancient Greek ἡμιστίχιον (hēmistíkhion).
Borrowed from Latin haemorrhagia, from Ancient Greek αἱμορραγία (haimorrhagía, “violent bleeding”), from αἷμα (haîma, “blood”) + ῥήγνυμι (rhḗgnumi, “to break asunder, to tear, to shatter”).

Inherited from Old Spanish fenchir, enchir, from Vulgar Latin *implīre, from Latin implēre. More information According to Coromines & Pascual, the initial f- in Old Spanish was likely due to phonetic and semantic similarities with finchar > modern hinchar. In dwindling use by the 16th century, hench
Inherited from Old Spanish fender, from Latin findere, findō, from Proto-Italic *findō, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeyd- (“to split”).

parole.significato: small groove, slit or other indentation
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *findicula, from Latin findō (“to cleave, to split, to divide”).
Inherited from Latin fēnīle.
Inherited from Latin fēnum, early monophthongized variant of faenum, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁(y)-no-, from *dʰeh₁(y)-. Compare English fennel and fenugreek.
Borrowed from Late Latin heptagōnus, borrowed from Ancient Greek ἑπτάγωνος (heptágōnos), from ἑπτά (heptá, “seven”) + γωνίᾱ (gōníā, “corner, angle”) + -ος (-os).
From Latin hepaticus, from Ancient Greek ἡπατικός (hēpatikós, “related to the liver”), from ἧπαρ (hêpar), ἥπατος (hḗpatos).
Inherited from Old Spanish herbadgo, hervadgo, ervadgo (c. 1257), Early Medieval Latin herbāticum, from Latin herba (“grass”). By surface analysis, hierba + -azgo. Doublet of herbaje.
Borrowed from Latin herbāceus (“grassy”).
Learned borrowing from Latin herbivorus. By surface analysis, Latin herba + Latin -i + Latin vorō.
Inherited from Old Spanish heredad, from Latin hērēditātem.
Inherited from Latin hērēditāre.
Inherited from Old Spanish heredero, from Latin hērēditārius, from hēres (“heir”).
Borrowed from Latin hērēditārius.
Borrowed from Latin haeresis, from Ancient Greek αἵρεσις (haíresis, “choice, system of principles”).

Inherited from Old Spanish herencia, a semi-learned borrowing from Latin haerentia, an irregular derivation from Latin hēres. The inherited Old Spanish herença didn't survive into modern Spanish. Compare Ladino erensya, Portuguese herança, Galician herdanza.

parole.significato: to wound, injure (cause physical injury and pain)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish ferir, from Latin feriō, -īre (“to hit”). Related to English interfere.
Inherited from Old Spanish ermana, from Latin germāna.
Inherited from Latin germānitātem.
Inherited from Old Spanish ermano, from Vulgar Latin *germānus (“brother”), from Latin germānus (“of a brother or sister”). Compare English germane. Displaced Old Spanish fradre, from fratēr.
From Old Spanish fermoso, from Latin fōrmōsus.
Borrowed from Latin hernia (“protruded viscus”).
From Latin hērōicus.
Borrowed from Latin hērōīna, from Late Ancient Greek ἡρωΐνη (hērōḯnē).
From herrar (“to horseshoe”), from hierro (“iron”), from Latin ferrum (“iron”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin ferrāmenta, from the plural of Latin ferrāmentum.
Inherited from Old Spanish ferrero, from Latin ferrārius (“smith, blacksmith”), from ferrum (“iron”). Equivalent to hierro + -ero.
Inherited from Latin ferrūmine.
Inherited from Old Spanish ferrén, ferraine, from Latin farrāgō via a Vulgar Latin form *ferrāgō, ferrāginem.
From hirviente, from Latin fervēns.

Inherited from Old Spanish fervir, from Latin fervēre, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰrewh₁- (“be hot, boil”). The change in verb class could be by analogy with servir and vivir. Cognate with English brew.
From Latin fervor.

Borrowed from Medieval Latin, Ecclesiastical Latin haereticus, from Ancient Greek αἱρετικός (hairetikós, “able to choose”), in Ecclesiastical Greek (“heretic”), from αἱρετίζω (hairetízō, “to choose”). Doublet of hereje.
From Latin haesitātiōnem.
From Latin haesitāre.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin heterogeneus, from Ancient Greek ἑτερογενής (heterogenḗs, “of different kinds”), from ἕτερος (héteros, “other, another, different”) + γένος (génos, “kind”).

Borrowed from Late Latin heteroclitus, from Ancient Greek ἑτερόκλιτος (heteróklitos), from ἕτερος (héteros, “other, another, different”) + κλίνω (klínō, “lean, incline”), the latter from Proto-Indo-European *ḱley-.
From Latin hexagōnum, from Ancient Greek ἑξάγωνον (hexágōnon).
From Latin faex, faecem.
Inherited from Old Spanish *fennir, from Latin fingere. See also the borrowed doublet fingir.

parole.significato: hiatus (a syllable break between two vowels, without an intervening consonant)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin hiātus (“opening”).
From Latin hībernālis.
Borrowed from Latin hībernāre. Doublet of invernar.
From Latin hibiscum.
Borrowed from Latin hydra, from Ancient Greek ὕδρα (húdra).
Borrowed from Latin hydrophobia, from Ancient Greek ὑδροφοβία (hudrophobía), equivalent to hidro- + -fobia.
From Late Latin hydromantia, from Ancient Greek ὑδρομαντεία (hudromanteía); corresponding to hidro- + -mancia.
Inherited from Latin hydromel.
Inherited from Old Spanish ydropisia, from Late Latin hydropisia, from Latin hydropisis, from Ancient Greek ὕδρωψ (húdrōps, “edema”), from ὕδωρ (húdōr, “water”). Compare with English dropsy.
Borrowed from Latin hydraulicus, borrowed from Ancient Greek ὑδραυλικός (hudraulikós), from ὕδραυλις (húdraulis, “water organ”) + -ικός (-ikós).
Borrowed from Latin hydropicus.
Inherited from Latin hedera, possibly from Proto-Indo-European *gʰed- (“to seize, grasp, take”).
Inherited from Old Spanish fiel, from Vulgar Latin *felem m or f, from Latin fel n.
From earlier yelo, from Latin gelū, from Proto-Indo-European *gel- (“cold”). Compare English gel.
Borrowed from Latin hiemālis.
Learned borrowing from Latin hyaena.
Inherited from Latin diāria.

parole.significato: grass (plant of the family Poaceae or plant that resembles grasses)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish yerva, from Latin herba. Compare Catalan herba, Portuguese erva.

Inherited from Old Spanish fierro, from Latin ferrum. Doublet of fierro (“branding iron”, inherited from Latin) and ferro (“anchor of a galley”, probably borrowed from Catalan). Other Romance cognates include French fer, Italian ferro, Portuguese ferro, and Romanian fier.

Borrowed from Latin hieraticus, from Ancient Greek ἱερατικός (hieratikós), from ἱερατεία (hierateía, “priesthood”), from ἱερατεύω (hierateúō, “be a priest”), from ἱερεύς (hiereús, “priest”), from ἱερός (hierós, “sacred”).
Inherited from Old Spanish figo, from Latin fīcus (“fig, fig tree”). Cognate with English fig.
Inherited from Old Spanish figuera, from Latin fīcāria, from fīcus (“fig”).
Inherited from Old Spanish fija, from Latin fīlia.
Inherited from Late Latin fīliastrum, from Latin fīlius. Compare Italian figliastro, Romanian fiastru.
Inherited from Old Spanish fijo, from Latin fīlius.
Inherited from Late Latin fīlāre. Derivable from hilo + -ar.
Borrowed from Latin hilaritas.
Borrowed from Latin hīlum.
From Latin hymēn, from Ancient Greek ὑμήν (humḗn, “skin; membrane”).
Borrowed from Latin hymnus, from Ancient Greek ὕμνος (húmnos, “song, hymn”).

From earlier fincar, from Old Spanish fincar, from Vulgar Latin *fīg(i)cāre, frequentative based on Latin fīgere (“drive in, fix in place”). Doublet of ficar. The /n/ may be due to the influence of Latin fingere and its derivatives.

parole.significato: to inflate or fill with air or liquid
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish finchar, from Latin īnflāre (“to inflate something, blow into it”). The phonetic development involved consonant spread of the medial [f], namely via *hinhláɾe or *finfláɾe, cf. hallar, and see also henchir. Doublet of borrowed inflar. Cognate with English inflate, Portugue

From hinchar + -zón (found in Old Spanish as finchazón), possibly corresponding to Latin īnflātiōnem, and therefore a doublet of inflación. Compare Portuguese inchação, Italian enfiagione, dialectal French enflaison, archaic Romanian umflăciune.
Inherited from Latin genesta. Doublet of genista.
Inherited from Old Spanish finojo, from Vulgar Latin *fenuclum, from Latin fēnuculum, from a diminutive of Latin fēnum.

parole.significato: knee (joint or the region of the joint in the middle part of the leg between the thigh and the shank)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish ynojo, from Late Latin genuculum, alteration of Latin geniculum, diminutive of genū (“knee”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ǵónu.

parole.significato: a kneading table; a table in which dough is kneaded
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *finctōrium, from *finctum + -ōrium, from Latin fictum.
Borrowed from Late Latin hypnōticus, from Ancient Greek ὑπνωτικός (hupnōtikós, “inducing sleep, soporific”).

Borrowed from Late Latin hippocampus (“sea horse”), from Ancient Greek ἱππόκαμπος (hippókampos, “sea horse, hippocamp”, from ἵππος (híppos, “horse”) + κάμπος (kámpos, “sea monster”)), describing a mythological creature with a horse's forepart and a fishlike hindquarter.
Borrowed from Latin hypocaustum, from Ancient Greek ὑπόκαυστον (hupókauston), from Ancient Greek ὑπό (hupó, “underneath”) + καίειν (kaíein, “to light a fire, burn”).

Borrowed from Late Latin hypocrisis, from Ancient Greek ὑπόκρισις (hupókrisis, “answer, stage acting, pretense”), from ῠ̔ποκρῑ́νομαι (hŭpokrī́nomai, “to reply”), from ὑπό (hupó, “under, hypo-”) + the middle voice of κρῑ́νω (krī́nō, “to separate, to judge, to decide”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin hippopotamus, from Ancient Greek ἱπποπόταμος (hippopótamos, “river horse”).
From Latin hypotheca, from Ancient Greek ὑποθήκη (hupothḗkē). Compare Scottish English hypothec.
Borrowed from New Latin hypothermia, from Ancient Greek ὑπο- (hupo-, “under”) + θέρμη (thérmē, “heat”) + Latin -ia. By surface analysis, hipo- + -termia.
From Scientific Latin hypoxia, from Ancient Greek ὑπο- (hupo-), English oxygen and -ia.
From Latin hyperbaton, from Ancient Greek ὑπερβατόν (huperbatón, “overstepping”), from ὑπέρ (hupér, “over”) + βαίνω (baínō, “to go, move, walk”).
From Latin hyperbolē, from Ancient Greek ὑπερβολή (huperbolḗ, “excess, exaggeration”), from ὑπέρ (hupér, “above”) + βάλλω (bállō, “to throw”). Doublet of hipérbola.
From Ecclesiastical Latin hypocrita, from Ancient Greek ὑποκριτής (hupokritḗs, “actor, hypocrite”), from ὑποκρίνομαι (hupokrínomai, “to answer, act, feign”).
Borrowed from Latin hippodromos, from Ancient Greek ἱππόδρομος (hippódromos), from ἵππος (híppos, “horse”) + δρόμος (drómos, “course”).
Borrowed from Late Latin hypothesis, from Ancient Greek ὑπόθεσις (hupóthesis, “base, basis of an argument”).
Borrowed from Latin Hyrcānus.
From Latin feriēns, feriēntem.
Borrowed from Latin hirsūtus.
From Latin hirūdō.
Inherited from Latin ferventem. Doublet of ferviente.
Borrowed from Latin hȳsōpum, hyssōpum, from Ancient Greek ὕσσωπος (hússōpos), from some Semitic source. See the Greek term for more information. Cognate with English hyssop.
Borrowed from Latin Hispalēnsis, from Hispalis (“Seville”) + -ēnsis (“-ese”), equivalent to Spanish + -ense.
Borrowed from Latin Hispānus, from Hispānia + -ānus.
Borrowed from Latin hispanicus, from Hispānia.
Borrowed from Latin historia, from Ancient Greek ἱστορία (historía).
Borrowed from Latin histrio.
From Latin histriōnicus.
From Latin hystericus, from Ancient Greek ὑστερικός (husterikós), from ὑστέρα (hustéra, “womb”). See histeria.
From Latin historicus.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin fīctus, variant of Latin fīxus, perfect passive participle of fīgō. Doublet of fijo. Compare Catalan fita and Portuguese fito.

parole.significato: Traditional New Mexican Spanish variant of hijo.
parole.testo: From the diminutive of hijo (hijito), with apheresis, from Old Spanish fijo, from Latin fīlius (“son”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁y-li-os (“sucker”), a derivation from the verbal root *dʰeh₁(y)- (“to suck”). Spelled as hito, rather than the expected jito, due to confluence of English and Spanis

parole.significato: from or relative to today, nowaday, current, present, present-day
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin hodiernus.
Inherited from Old Spanish fogar, from Vulgar Latin focāris, from Latin focus. Compare Galician fogar, English foyer.

Inherited from Old Spanish hogaça, from Late Latin focācium (via its plural focācia), derived from Latin focus (“hearth”). Compare Portuguese fogaça. Doublet of focaccia, which was borrowed from Italian.
Inherited from Latin hōc annō, ablative of hic + annus (“this year”). Compare Portuguese ogano and Asturian anguaño.

Inherited from Old Spanish foguera, from Vulgar Latin *focāria, a nominalization of Latin focārius (“of or relating to hearths”), from focus (“fire”) + -ārius. Compare Portuguese fogueira, Catalan foguera, Italian focaia, Romanian focar, English foyer.

parole.significato: leaf (usually green and flat organ that is the most prominent feature of most vegetative plants)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish foja, from Late Latin folia, the plural of Classical Latin folium (“leaf”) reinterpreted as a feminine singular noun. Doublet of folio, borrowed from Latin. Cognate with Portuguese folha, Catalan fulla, French feuille, and English foil.
From hojalde, from Latin foliātilis (panis) (literally “bread of leaves”).
Inherited from Old Spanish folgar, from Late Latin follicāre (“to pant, blow, breathe”), from Latin follis (“bellows”) whence English fool and folly.
From follar, from Vulgar Latin *fullāre, from Latin fullo (“fuller”).

parole.significato: the skin or membrane covering some fruits and seeds, such as grapes, beans, etc.
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *folliclu, from Latin folliculus, diminutive form of follis (“purse, sack”). Compare the borrowed doublet folículo. Cognate with Portuguese folhelho.
Inherited from Old Spanish follín, from Vulgar Latin *fullīginem (compare the attested follīginem), from Latin fūlīginem, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰuh₂li-, from *dʰewh₂-.
Borrowed from Late Latin holocaustum, from Ancient Greek ὁλόκαυστος (holókaustos).

Inherited from Old Spanish omne, from Latin hominem, homō, from Old Latin hemō, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰmṓ (“earthling”). The Old Spanish form omne was first dissimilated to omre and then a gliding sound -b- arose before the -r-. Compare the same development in cumbre, hembra, nombre, hambre, co
Inherited from Old Spanish ombro, from Latin humerus, umerus, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₃émsos (“shoulder”). Doublet of húmero.
From Latin homicīda.
Inherited from Old Spanish omicidio, omizidio, homicidio, homizidio, homiçidio, omeçidio, borrowed from Latin homicīdium. It replaced the inherited variant omezillo, omecillo in Old Spanish.
From Late Latin homīlia.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin homogeneus, from Ancient Greek ὁμογενής (homogenḗs, “of the same race, family or kind”), from ὁμός (homós, “same”) + γένος (génos, “kind”).
Borrowed from Latin homologāre, equivalent to homólogo + -ar.
From Latin Homēricus, from Homērus (“Homer”).
From Latin homunculus.
Inherited from Old Spanish fonda, from Latin funda.

Inherited from Old Spanish fondo, from Latin fundus, with the Latin noun taking on an adjectival sense in Spanish.  PIE word  *bʰudʰmḗn An alternative theory sees the Old Spanish fondo as a shortening of an earlier, pre-literary *perfondo, from the Latin adjective profundus instead, which matches wi
From hondo + -ura, from Latin fundus.
Inherited from Old Spanish onestat, from Latin honestatem.

Inherited from Old Spanish onestat, onestad, from Latin honestātem. The ending was altered to conform to the common suffix -idad; according to Coromines and Pascual, first attested in this new form in the 15th century, in a work of Alfonso de Palencia.
Borrowed from Latin honestus, an adjective based on honor.
Inherited from Old Spanish onor, from Latin honōrem.
Borrowed from Latin honōrābilis. Equivalent to honor + -able.
Borrowed from Latin honorāre. Compare the inherited honrar.
From Latin honōrārius.
From Latin honōrificus.
Inherited from Old Spanish onrra, onra, derived from onrrar + -a, the former from Latin honōrāre.
Inherited from Old Spanish hondrado, from Latin honorātus.
Inherited from Old Spanish hondrar, onrrar, onrar, from Latin honōrāre. Doublet of honorar, which was borrowed.
Borrowed from Latin hoplītēs m, from Ancient Greek ὁπλῑ́της (hoplī́tēs, “hoplite”).

parole.significato: hour (a time period of sixty minutes)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin hōra (“hour”).
Borrowed from Latin Horātiānus, from Horātius.

parole.significato: a hole or other perforation that crosses something from side to side, or that crosses all of its parts
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin forātum < forātus (“drilled, pierced”), perfect passive participle of forō.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin horārius.
Inherited from Old Spanish forca, from Latin furca.
Borrowed from Latin hordeum.
Borrowed from Latin horizontem, from Ancient Greek ὁρίζων (horízōn).
Inherited from Latin fōrma. Compare the borrowed doublet forma.

Inherited from an ellipsis of Late Latin pariēs fōrmācea (“a moulded wall”), from fōrmāceus, in reference to its being made by stuffing between two boards. Related to Ancient Greek μορφή (morphḗ, “a shape, form”). Reflects pared's change of gender from the original masculine. Compare hormazo and hor
Inherited from Late Latin fōrmācium, substantivised from fōrmāceus (“made in a mould”), related to Ancient Greek μορφή (morphḗ, “a shape, form”). Compare hormaza and horma (“dry stone wall”).
Inherited from Old Spanish formiga, from Latin formīca.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *formīcārium, from Latin formīca. Compare Portuguese formigueiro, Catalan formiguer, Italian formicaio, Romanian furnicar.

parole.significato: a meat pie made with pork loin, chorizo and hard-boiled eggs
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *fornāceus, from Latin fornāx (“oven”).
From horno + -ear, from Old Spanish forno, from Latin furnus.

From horno + -illo (diminutive suffix); possibly corresponds to a Vulgar Latin *furnellus, from Latin furnus. Compare French fourneau, Italian fornello, Catalan fornell, Galician Fornelos (toponym), Occitan fornèl, Sicilian furneddu.
Inherited from Old Spanish forno, from Latin furnus.
Borrowed from Latin horrendus.
Borrowed from Latin horribilis.
Borrowed from Late Latin horripilare.

Borrowed from Latin horrorem. Cf. also the popular Old Spanish horrura, inherited from a derivative of the Latin or with a change of suffix, and taking on the meaning of "dirtiness, filth, impurity, scum"; comparable to derivatives of horridus in other Romance languages, like Italian ordo, Old Frenc
Borrowed from New Latin Hortensia, from Hortense de Beauharnais, from whom the flower is named after.

parole.significato: horticulture (art or science of cultivating gardens)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin *horticultūra.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin horoscopus, from Ancient Greek ὡροσκόπος (hōroskópos), from ὥρα (hṓra, “any limited time”) + σκοπός (skopós, “watcher”).
Inherited from Latin fuscus (compare Portuguese fosco, fusco, Italian fosco, Catalan fosc, Old French fusque).

parole.significato: to host (to perform the role of a host)
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Latin hospitāre (or hospitor, hospitārī), from Latin hospes.
Borrowed from Latin hospitium, from hospes (“host, guest”).
Borrowed from Late Latin hospitāle (“hospice, shelter, guesthouse”), from Latin hospitālis (“hospitable”). Doublet of hostal.
Borrowed from Latin hospitalitātem, from hospitālis (“hospitable”), from hospes (“host, guest”).
Early borrowing from Ecclesiastical Latin hostia (“host, consecrated bread ← victim, sacrifice”). Compare Italian ostia, French ostie.
Inherited from Old Spanish fostigar, from Late Latin fūstīgāre, from Latin fūstis. Doublet of fustigar, a borrowing.
Borrowed from Latin hostīlis.
Borrowed from Latin hostīlitātem.
Inherited from Latin fautus.
Inherited from Old Spanish oy, from Latin hodiē. Cognate with Portuguese hoje, and Italian oggi.
Inherited from Latin fovea. Doublet of fóvea.
Inherited from Latin fovea, with a change in gender or possibly through a Vulgar Latin form *foveum. Compare Portuguese fojo, Galician foxo, Asturian fueyu.
Inherited from Old Spanish foz, from Latin falcem.
Inherited from Old Spanish foç, from Latin fōcem, early monophthongized variant of faucem.

parole.significato: to root, dig with the snout
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *fodiāre, from Latin fodere (“to dig”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰod- (“to pierce, dig”).

parole.significato: acre; as much land as can be ploughed in a day
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish huebra, from Latin opera. See also obra, which was influenced by the verb obrar. Also a doublet of ópera, a borrowing from Italian.
Derived from an Old Spanish verb ocar or aocar, from the Latin occāre (“to harrow”) (whence also Portuguese oco), from Latin occa. Related to German Egge.
Deverbal from holgar, from Late Latin follicāre (“to blow”), from Latin follis. Compare Portuguese folga (“rest; day off”). Doublet of juerga.
Inherited from Old Spanish huerco (“Hell; the Devil”), from Latin Orcus (“the underworld; the god Pluto”). Cognate with English ogre and orc. Doublet of orco and ogro.
Inherited from Latin hortus. Cognate with Ladino guerta.
Inherited from Latin hortus, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰortós.
Inherited from Latin fossa. See also fosa, borrowed from the same source.

Inherited from Old Spanish huesso, from Latin ossum, popular variant of os, ossis, from Proto-Italic *ōs, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₃ésth₁ (“bone”), *h₂óst. Compare Catalan os, French os, Interlingua osso, Italian osso, Portuguese osso, Romanian os, Sardinian ossu. Political sense comes

Inherited from Latin hostem (“enemy, stranger”), from Proto-Italic *hostim, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰóstim (“guest, stranger”). Compare Catalan host (“army”), Italian oste (“army, host”), Romanian oaste (“army, host”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *ŏva f sg (“roe”), from Latin ōva n pl (“eggs”). Doublet of huevo (“egg”), from the Latin singular ōvum. Compare Portuguese ova.
Inherited from Old Spanish hueuo, from Vulgar Latin *ŏvum, from Classical Latin ōvum, from Proto-Italic *ōw(j)om, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ōwyóm, from *h₂éwis, possibly from *h₂ew-.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *fugītīcius, from Latin fugere (“flee”). By surface analysis, huido + -izo.

Inherited from Old Spanish fuir~foir, from Vulgar Latin *fugīre, from Latin fugere, fugiō, from Proto-Italic *fugiō, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰewg-. Cognate with French fuir, Portuguese fugir, Galician fuxir, Asturian afuxir, Catalan fugir.
From Latin hūmānus, from homō (“human being”).
Inherited from Latin fūmāre. Doublet of fumar.
Inherited from Old Spanish fumeyar, inherited from Vulgar Latin *fūmizāre, from Latin fūmigāre. Derivable from humo + -ear. Doublet of fumigar, a borrowing from Latin.
First attested in 1498. Borrowed from Latin humectans, equivalent to humectar + -ante.
Learned borrowing from Latin humectāre.
Haplological contraction of Latin humiditātem.
From humiditas (“humedad (humithy) in Latin”) + -ificar.
Inherited from Old Spanish umildat, from Latin humilitātem. Equivalent to humilde + -dad.
Modified (after humildad) from Old Spanish humil, borrowed from Latin humilis.
Semi-learned borrowing from Late Latin humiliātiōnem, from humiliō (“to humiliate”).
Altered from Old Spanish homillar, a borrowing from Late Latin humiliāre.
Inherited from Old Spanish fumo, from Latin fūmus. Doublet of fumo. Compare Ladino umo.
Borrowed from Latin hūmōrem. Cognate with English humor.
Ultimately from Latin hūmorālis.
Inherited from Old Spanish fundir. Doublet of fundir (“to cast, melt”), from Latin fundere. Compare English found (“to cast metal”), founder (“to sink”).

Borrowed from Late Latin Hunnus, from Koine Greek Χοῦνοι (Khoûnoi) or Χουνοί (Khounoí), borrowed through Middle Iranian, apparently ultimately from Turkic *Hun-yü, the name of a tribe (they were known in China as Xiongnu). More at Huns.
From huro, ultimately from Latin forō. Compare Portuguese buraco, Galician buraco, furaco, Asturian buracu, furacu.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin forāneus (influenced in Spanish by hurón), ultimately from Latin forās (“outside”). Doublet of foráneo.
From Old Spanish furgar, from Vulgar Latin *fūricāre, from Latin fūr (“thief”) whence English ferret and furtive.
Inherited from Old Spanish furto. Cognate with English furtive.
Inherited from Late Latin fūrō, from Latin fūror (“to steal”) + -ō. Cognate with English ferret.
Inherited from Latin fūsus. Cognate with English fuse.
From Latin hui.
Inherited from Late Latin orphanus, from Ancient Greek ὀρφανός (orphanós, “without parents, fatherless”).  PIE word  *h₃órbʰos

Inherited from Old Spanish huésped, from Latin hospitem, from Proto-Italic *hostipotis, an old compound of hostis and the root of potis, possibly corresponding to a Proto-Indo-European root *gʰóstipotis, a compound of *gʰóstis and *pótis. Doublet of host. See also hueste.
Borrowed from New Latin, from hyrax + -aceum.
From Latin habilis (“suitable, skillful”). Cognate with English able.
Borrowed from Latin habitus.
Borrowed from Latin halitus.
Borrowed from Latin helīcem, from Ancient Greek ἕλῑξ (hélīx, “spiral”).
Borrowed from Latin hērōem, from Ancient Greek ἥρως (hḗrōs).
From Latin hibridus, hybridus (“hybrid”, adjective), from hibrida f (“hybrid”, noun), most likely from Ancient Greek, with influence from ὕβρις (húbris).
Inherited from Old Spanish figado, from Late Latin fīcatum, ellipsis of Latin iecur fīcātum (literally “figgy liver”), from fīcus (“fig”) + -ātum.
From Latin hispĭdus

Inherited from Old Spanish orrio, from Latin horreum, from Ancient Greek ὡρεῖον (hōreîon). The standard form in modern Spanish, with /e/ rather than /j/, appears to be the result of a latinizing modification. Compare Asturian horriu, horru and Catalan orri.
Borrowed from Latin horridus.
Borrowed from Latin hūmidus, variant of ūmidus.
Borrowed from Latin humerus. Doublet of hombro.

parole.significato: The ninth letter of the Spanish alphabet, written in the Latin script.
parole.testo: Directly from Latin.

parole.significato: unadapted form of ibídem (“ibidem”) (in the same place)
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin ibīdem.
From Latin ībis, from Ancient Greek ἶβις (îbis), from Egyptian hbj.

parole.significato: Iberian (of, from or relating to Iberia)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin Hibēricus (“Iberian”). First attested in late 16th century.
Borrowed from Latin ibidem.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin īconoclasta, from Ancient Greek εἰκονοκλάστης (eikonoklástēs, “breaker of images”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin īconographia, from Ancient Greek εἰκονογραφία (eikonographía), from εἰκών (eikṓn, “image, likeness”).
From Latin ictericus.
Learned borrowing from Latin idea, from Ancient Greek ἰδέα (idéa, “notion, pattern”), from εἴδω (eídō, “to see”). Compare Portuguese ideia.
From Latin ideālis.

Pseudo-Latinism, derived from idem (“same”) + potentia (“the quality of having power”), coined as a calque of English idempotence, equivalent to ídem + potencia. Cognate with Catalan idempotència, French idempotence, Italian idempotenza, Portuguese idempotência, and Romanian idempotență.
From Latin identitātem.
Borrowed from scholastic Medieval Latin identificāre, from Medieval Latin identicus, from Classical Latin idem (“same”), + Latin faciō. Cognate with English identify.
From Latin īdyllium, from Ancient Greek εἰδύλλιον (eidúllion), diminutive of εἶδος (eîdos, “shape, form”).
Borrowed from Late Latin idioma, from Ancient Greek ἰδίωμα (idíōma, “peculiarity; idiom”).
Borrowed from Latin idiōta, from Ancient Greek ἰδιώτης (idiṓtēs, “layman”) from ἴδιος (ídios, “private”).
From Latin idiōtismus.

From Medieval Latin identicus.

Borrowed from Latin idōneus. Cognate with English idoneous.
Inherited from Old Spanish eglesia (9th century), a semi-learned descendant of Vulgar Latin eclesia, from Latin ecclēsia, from Ancient Greek ἐκκλησία (ekklēsía, “assembly”).
From Latin ignārus.

Borrowed from Latin ignominia.
From Latin ignōminiōsus.

From Latin īgnōrante or īgnōrantī, singular ablative of īgnōrāns (“ignorant”).

parole.significato: to not know, be ignorant of
parole.testo: From Old Spanish ignorar, a learned borrowing from Latin ignōrāre. Doublet of añorar.
Learned borrowing from Latin ignōtus.
Inherited from Old Spanish igual~egual (both common in the 13th century), from Latin aequālis. Cognate with English equal.
Inherited from Latin aequālitātem, from aequālis (“equal, even”). By surface analysis, igual + -dad. Compare Catalan igualtat, French égalité, Portuguese igualdade.

parole.significato: synonym of ijar, side (region between the ribcage and the hip)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *īliāta, from Latin īlia, plural of īle (“guts, intestines”). Compare English ilium.

parole.significato: flank, side, region between the ribcage and the hip in mammals
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *īliāris, from Latin īlia, plural of īle (“guts, intestines”). Cognate with English ileum, Portuguese ilhal and ilharga.
From Latin illātiōnem.

From Latin illaesus.

From Latin imitātiōnem. Cognate with English imitation.
From Latin imitātor. Cognate with English imitator.

parole.significato: to imitate, to mimic, to ape, to copy, to copycat, to impersonate, to simulate
